For the TCGA PRAD mutation cohort, I treated “Pathogenic/Oncogenic alterations” as non-synonymous mutations in genes annotated by the MAF’s COSMIC Cancer Gene Census gene-level fields, because no per-variant OncoKB/ClinVar pathogenicity field was available.

Top mutated genes under this filter were TP53 (60/498, 12.0%), ATM (22/498, 4.4%), CHEK2 (21/498, 4.2%), PTEN (17/498, 3.4%), PIK3CA (14/498, 2.8%), CTNNB1 (13/498, 2.6%), KDM6A (13/498, 2.6%), NOTCH2 (11/498, 2.2%), APC (10/498, 2.0%), and SETD2 (10/498, 2.0%). Additional recurrent CGC-filtered genes included ARID2, BRCA2, and CDK12 (9/498 each, 1.8%).

I visualized the results as a ranked bar plot of the top mutated genes and an oncoplot-style mutation presence/absence matrix. The figure files are in outputs/da25_1/: top_pathogenic_oncogenic_mutated_genes_barplot.png/.svg and top_pathogenic_oncogenic_oncoplot_matrix.png/.svg.

For genomic association with T stage, I used pathologic T stage because it was more complete than clinical T stage. In 491 patients with mutation and pathologic T-stage data, I compared T2 organ-confined tumors (n=188) against T3/T4 extraprostatic or locally advanced tumors (n=303). Fisher exact tests with BH-FDR correction across 40 recurrent CGC-filtered genes found one significant association: TP53 mutations were enriched in T3/T4 tumors (49/303, 16.2%) compared with T2 tumors (11/188, 5.9%; odds ratio=3.10, Fisher p=5.88e-4, BH q=0.0235). No other tested gene remained significant after FDR correction.

Key limitation: this is a gene-level CGC proxy for pathogenic/oncogenic status, not a per-variant pathogenicity classification. It also excludes some known prostate cancer drivers such as SPOP and FOXA1 because they were not captured by the CGC annotations present in this MAF.
